discovery: Ultrasoft pseudopotential and projector augmented-wave methods enabling predictive first-principles electronic-structure calculations of real materials
subfield: Condensed matter physics / computational materials physics
motivation: Vanderbilt's ultrasoft pseudopotentials (1990) and Blöchl's projector augmented-wave method (1994) solved the central obstacle to accurate plane-wave density-functional calculations for transition metals, oxides and f-electron systems: representing localized valence states and all-electron information at tractable cost. Kresse turned these ideas into a rigorous, efficient framework, proving the formal link between ultrasoft and PAW approaches and embedding them in widely used codes. The consequence has been a transformation of physics practice: defect formation and migration energies, magnetism in iron alloys, phase stability of nuclear fuels, catalysis and battery materials are now computed with predictive accuracy before experiments are made. In radiation-damage physics, for example, first-principles data on point defects in bcc iron and Fe-Cr alloys underpin the multiscale models used to design steels for fission and fusion reactors. Few theoretical advances have so directly changed what experimentalists and engineers can measure, understand and build.
